```text
Peak Poker Performance

   ♠ Did the process I used to reduce tilt or other emotional
       symptom(s) work in the long run?
   ♠ What did the strategy cost me in money, health, vitality, or

   ♠ Did it bring me closer to achieving the kind of results I want in the

    Even if we don’t have these detrimental mental game issues, it’s likely
that we use control strategies like distraction, zoning out, or self-
criticism, all of which tend to backfire eventually. If the thoughts and
feelings you’re trying to control are minor, it usually works out just fine.
It’s only when we have very strong emotions or are in a very important or
intense situation that difficulty ensues. The reason why mental game is-
sues are so prevalent is because we tend to focus on the wrong things.
    Being able to manage yourself is not as much about controlling emo-
tions as it is about being open to them. It’s very difficult if not impossible
to purge or control emotions consistently for any period of time. Most
players would like to eliminate or control their strong emotions, but this is
almost always counterproductive. In your attempts to get rid of uncom-
fortable feelings, you end up struggling with them. Attention is diverted
from the game and placed on your internal state as unwanted emotions
are battled. How can you play effective poker when your attention is in-
wardly focused? How you respond to strong emotions as they arise is the
key to being a mentally tough poker player.
    Whenever people attempt to squelch troubling thoughts and feelings,
they tend to get worse. If you are trying to manage unwanted thoughts,
feelings, and images by avoiding them, you have fallen into psychological
quicksand. The more you avoid, the more solidly your brain will be fixated
on unwanted thoughts, feelings, and images.
    To determine whether or not avoidance is an issue for you, ask your-
self how often you engage in any of the following:
```

```text
   Note that avoidance behavior is a perfectly natural reaction to un-
pleasant thoughts and situations. There are even some cases where
avoiding certain situations or people is ideal. The trick is to figure out if
your avoidance tactics are helping or hurting you. As you gather your
data, remember not to judge or criticize yourself. This is merely a fact-
finding mission, and you’ll learn plenty of tactics later to help you change
any unhealthy thought patterns.

Emotion-Driven Behaviors
If you have played poker for any length of time, it’s likely that you have
experienced strong emotions, which have influenced you to play erratic-
ally. When our thinking is clouded through having strong emotions, we
tend to behave in non-optimal ways. Under such circumstances, you may
have racked up losses because you played too loose or too tight. Perhaps
you missed clear signals that running a multi-street bluff was not wise.
Regardless of your particular mistakes, there is no doubt that strong
emotions impacted your win rate. Once you are removed from the situa-
tion, you may even wonder why you made such an obvious mistake.
    Stressful times often lead to unwanted behaviors and psychologists
```

```text
                                          Common Psychological Hurdles

call this “emotion-driven behavior.” Typically, we know we are behaving
poorly, but we do it anyway because it provides temporary relief. Unfor-
tunately, the relief is only temporary and such behavior often impedes our
progress towards our long-term goals. In poker, “tilt” is a catch-all term
for a variety of emotion-driven behaviors. When you tilt, do you ever get
upset and then do things that have bad consequences for you? If so,
that’s emotion-driven behavior in a nutshell. You might be engaging in
emotion-driven behavior if you:

   ♠ say things you later regret
   ♠ act without thinking
   ♠ have trouble resisting temptations when stressed or otherwise on
       tilt
   ♠ do things that have bad consequences.

    To better understand why we do these things, it’s important to under-
stand what emotions are and how they work. There are over 500 words
in the English language describing various emotions (e.g. sadness, anger,
fear, envy, disappointment), and there are a number of synonyms for
each major emotion. Even though we have lots of labels for emotions,
they are hard for most people to describe, in part because they seem
subjective.
    There’s a pretty wide variation in the ways people relate to and ex-
press their emotions. They come and go and tend to be of short duration,
lasting from seconds to minutes, unless we are subjected to prolonged
circumstances or engage in rumination. If they go on for an extended pe-
riod of time, they are more accurately called moods, which tend to be less
intense than emotions. For example, you can be in a grumpy mood for a
day or two, but a full blown fit of rage typically lasts only a few minutes at
most.
    Emotional styles are individualized and some people feel things more
strongly than others. Some people tend to be more positive and others
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

more negative, on the whole.
  Emotions are easier to understand if we break them down into their
component parts:

   ♠ Physiological sensations occur with our emotions. Anger can bring
       a heated face and clenched muscles. Anxiety is often accompanied
       by sweaty palms, a racing heart, and muscle tension. Notice that
       excitement brings along the same physiological sensations as
       anxiety.
   ♠ Thoughts accompany our emotions either as words or phrases or
       as images. If you feel anger, it is typical to imagine angry scenarios.
       If you feel sad, you may have negative thoughts such as “Things
       never work out for me.”
   ♠ Urges are the final piece of the puzzle. These are our desires to
       behave in a certain way. When we take a bad beat, we may have
       the urge to yell, curse, or throw something. When we act in
       accordance with these urges our behavior is emotionally driven.


   As you can see, emotions trigger sensations in the body, thoughts in
the mind, and urges to act in certain ways. We need to become aware of
our emotions so we can decide if they are helpful or not in a given situa-
tion. To increase your self-awareness complete the tracking tools shown
in Table 6 or Table 7 whenever you have a strong emotional reaction.
Tracking your responses will offer you a much clearer picture of whether
or not your emotional reactions are helpful.
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

Self-Criticism
The final mental game leak I want to explore is self-criticism. People who
engage in self-criticism have an inner voice that responds to perceived
mistakes or misdeeds very harshly. They say to themselves things like “I
am a loser” or “How could I be such an idiot!?” You may be a self-criticizer
if you:

   ♠ call yourself names
   ♠ criticize yourself harshly for things you have said or done
   ♠ blame yourself for your failures while not taking credit for your
       successes
   ♠ are intolerant of perceived weaknesses or flaws.

    To be clear, there is benefit to constructive criticism, but that’s not
what I’m describing here. This sort of self-criticism is one-sided, judg-
mental, and insulting. People who use self-criticism typically believe that
it will lead to better self-discipline, but studies show this style actually
impedes goal pursuit and can lead to procrastination. Researchers hy-
pothesize that harsh self-criticism leads to emotions like shame, guilt, an-
ger, embarrassment, sadness, and even hopelessness, which results in low
morale and lack of confidence. Self-criticism is also associated with higher
levels of anxiety.
    If you have been treating yourself this way for a long time it has likely
become a habit. Habitual thinking patterns pop into our heads randomly.
To find out if you’re caught in this thinking trap, use Table 8 to collect
some data over a period of time to get an accurate depiction of the ex-
tent of the problem as well as any associated patterns.
```
